findings.explanation:
Salesforce maintains indexes on a documented set of standard fields: RecordTypeId, Division, CreatedDate, Systemmodstamp, Name, Email (on contacts and leads), lookup and master-detail foreign keys, and the record Id, which is the primary key for every object. Of the choices, Name, SystemModstamp, and RecordType appear on that list without qualification, so those are the three to pick.
CreatedBy is not on it. What carries the index is CreatedDate, the timestamp — not CreatedById.
One caveat about the remaining option. The Large Data Volumes guide writes that entry as "Systemmodstamp (LastModifiedDate)", treating the two as the same index rather than presenting LastModifiedDate as unindexed. So LastModifiedDate is not a clean distractor: this item works because the three fields named above are unambiguous, not because filtering on LastModifiedDate is documented to miss an index.
findings.note: Answer A,C,E stands, but the explanation asserted that LastModifiedDate is not indexed. The LDV Indexes page lists the field as "Systemmodstamp (LastModifiedDate)", which implies the opposite. Rewritten to justify the three picks from what the list states outright, and to flag option D as an unreliable distractor rather than a documented negative.

findings.explanation:
COUNT() asks the database for a number rather than for records, and the Apex Developer Guide is precise about what that costs: for COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName), limits are counted as one query row — unless the query carries a GROUP BY, in which case one query row per grouping is consumed. So counting millions of Opportunities spends a single row against the 50,000-row query limit.
The same passage is what really rules out SUM(). Every aggregate function other than COUNT() and COUNT(fieldName) counts each row used by the aggregation as a query row, so SUM() over millions of Opportunities would exceed the 50,000-row limit outright — quite apart from totalling a currency field instead of counting records. A SOQL for loop retrieves the records it iterates, and a batch job is asynchronous and far heavier than one query for a number the component needs in order to render.

BatchApexErrorEvent is a standard platform event that the platform publishes on your behalf. The Apex Developer Guide states that if the start, execute, or finish method of a batch Apex job encounters an unhandled exception, a BatchApexErrorEvent is fired, and that to get this behaviour the batch class declaration must implement the Database.RaisesPlatformEvents marker interface. The event's own reference page then settles the rest of the option set in a single line: "Only the Salesforce Platform can fire this event; Apex code and the API can't." That rules out every option built on publishing the event yourself, whether the option calls the event custom or standard.
The same page lists the supported subscribers as Apex triggers, flows, processes, the Pub/Sub API, and the Streaming API (CometD), so an external system genuinely can listen on the /event/BatchApexErrorEvent channel. It receives the AsyncApexJob id, the exception type and message, the stack trace, and the record ids that were in scope at the time of failure.
There is also a reason no custom-event design could have worked here. An unhandled exception is by definition not caught, so there is no point in your own code at which to publish, and an event published with the default publish-after-commit behaviour is discarded when the transaction rolls back. addError() adds a record-level error inside a trigger and publishes nothing at all.

Two things make this test runnable. Enqueue the job between Test.startTest() and Test.stopTest(): a queueable is asynchronous, and the platform runs everything queued inside that block synchronously once Test.stopTest() is reached, so assertions placed afterwards actually see the job's results. And guard the chained enqueue: OrderQueueableJob calls System.enqueueJob again from inside execute(), and chaining a further job during a test run raises an error, so the standard pattern is to wrap that inner enqueue in a Test.isRunningTest() check and let the chain stop at the first link under test.
The other two options address nothing. SeeAllData=true widens data access and has no bearing on asynchronous execution — there is no "bulk mode" for a queueable to run in. View All on Order changes what the running user can see, which is not why the test fails.
Worth knowing: the chaining-in-a-test restriction is long-standing platform behaviour but is no longer stated on the Queueable Apex page. What that page does document is that only one job can be enqueued from an executing job, and the startTest/stopTest pattern this answer relies on.

With SeeAllData=true the query can see the org's existing records, so it returns all six accounts whose name starts with "Test" — the five already there plus the one the test inserted — and the delete removes that whole list. Both assertions therefore pass while the test is running.
None of it survives. The Apex Developer Guide is explicit that the annotation applies to data queries but does not apply to record creation or changes, including deletions, and that new and changed records are still rolled back in Apex tests even when the annotation is used. So the org is back to its original five "Test" accounts once the test finishes: the deletion is undone and the inserted sixth account does not persist either. The test does not fail, which is what makes the count — not an error — the thing the question is asking about.

A trigger runs synchronously, and Salesforce does not permit a synchronous callout from trigger context — attempting one raises "Callout from triggers are currently not supported". The only way to call a web service from a trigger is to hand the work to asynchronous Apex: an @future(callout=true) method or a Queueable. That makes this a use case where synchronous Apex is not merely slower but forbidden.
Processing high volumes and updating a record after an insert are both done synchronously every day; volume pushes you toward Batch Apex for governor headroom, not because a synchronous approach is impossible.
Option A is the weak distractor here and worth naming: scheduling a batch to run later does require the Schedulable interface, which is itself asynchronous Apex, so read literally it is also something "only performed by asynchronous Apex". The discriminator the item is reaching for is the callout, where a synchronous attempt is actively rejected by the platform rather than merely unavailable.
